# Osgood-Schlatter disease

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Pediatrics > Pediatric orthopedics and trauma > Osgood-Schlatter disease*

[Original Article Link](/library/rQ0fxf)

---

## Summary

Osgood-Schlatter disease (OSD) is a <u>traction apophysitis</u> that occurs where the <u>patellar tendon</u> attaches to the <u>tibial tuberosity</u>. It is an overuse injury typically seen in children aged 9–14 years of age who regularly engage in athletics. OSD is characterized by progressive <u>anterior</u> <u>knee pain</u> that is exacerbated by activity (typically jumping, kneeling, running, or squatting). On examination, there is usually focal swelling and tenderness over the <u>tibial tuberosity</u>. Diagnosis is clinical. Imaging is reserved for ruling out differential diagnoses of OSD if there is diagnostic uncertainty. Treatment is usually conservative, involving <u>NSAIDs</u>, ice, and <u>physical therapy</u>. <u>Surgery</u> is reserved for refractory cases in patients with a closed <u>growth plate</u>.

---

## Epidemiology

* Age

* <u>Adolescents</u>; on average 9–14 years old

* Commonly develops shortly after <u>growth spurts</u>

* Sex: <u>♂</u> > <u>♀</u> (3:1)




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

* Overuse (especially sports involving sprinting and jumping) during the <u>ossification</u> period (<u>adolescence</u>) → excessive strain and repeated avulsion of the <u>patellar ligament</u> on the <u>tibial tuberosity</u> → inflammation → <u>traction</u> <u>apophysitis</u>

* <u>Chronic inflammation</u> of the <u>patellar ligament</u> can disrupt the secondary <u>ossification</u> of the <u>tibial tuberosity</u> → detachment of the <u>apophysis</u> → subsequent <u>callus</u> formation during the healing process → persistently prominent <u>tibial tuberosity</u> [[1]](/library/jMa_oO)

## Clinical features

### Symptoms [[2]](/library/iAWJjL0)[[3]](/library/kHWmq50)




* Progressive <u>anterior</u> <u>knee pain</u>

* Exacerbated by activity, e.g., jumping, kneeling, running, squatting

* Relieved by rest (within minutes to hours after activity)

* Often unilateral  [[3]](/library/kHWmq50)





### Examination findings [[2]](/library/iAWJjL0)[[3]](/library/kHWmq50)




* Focal swelling and tenderness of the <u>tibial tuberosity</u>  [[3]](/library/kHWmq50)

* <u>Pain</u> is reproduced by knee extension against resistance.

* Tightness of the <u>quadriceps</u> and <u>hamstrings</u>





![Tibial tuberosity in Osgood-Schlatter disease](media/xy34a7906r1jb786m8jv5vfp.jpg)

## Diagnosis

OSD is usually a <u>clinical diagnosis</u>; imaging is indicated to rule out differential diagnoses of OSD if there is diagnostic uncertainty. [[4]](/library/CGWqYM0)




### Imaging [[4]](/library/CGWqYM0)[[5]](/library/KHWUr50)




#### Modalities [[4]](/library/CGWqYM0)




* <u>X-ray</u> (first-line): AP, <u>lateral</u>, and <u>tangential patella views</u>    [[4]](/library/CGWqYM0)[[1]](/library/jMa_oO)[[5]](/library/KHWUr50)

* <u>MRI</u> without IV contrast: Consider if initial radiographs are normal.

* <u>Ultrasound</u>: not routinely indicated  [[4]](/library/CGWqYM0)[[6]](/library/py1LTj0)





#### Findings




In acute disease, imaging shows signs of inflammation (e.g., <u>soft tissue</u> swelling); in subacute and chronic (> 3 months) disease, abnormalities are seen in the bones and/or <u>tendons</u>. [[3]](/library/kHWmq50)[[7]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




* Findings common to all modalities [[5]](/library/KHWUr50)[[8]](/library/j_W_LL0)

* <u>Anterior</u> <u>soft tissue</u> swelling

* Prominent <u>tibial tuberosity</u> over the tibial shaft [[9]](/library/P_WWoL0)

* Irregular or fragmented <u>tibial tuberosity</u>   [[9]](/library/P_WWoL0)[[10]](/library/kAWmPL0)

* Formation of free <u>ossicles</u>

* Calcification and thickening of the <u>patellar tendon</u>

* Specific findings by modality

* <u>X-ray</u>: blurred margins of the <u>patellar tendon</u>  [[5]](/library/KHWUr50)

* <u>MRI</u> [[3]](/library/kHWmq50)

* <u>Edema</u> around the <u>tibial tuberosity</u>

* Partial tears in the <u>apophysis</u>

* Infrapatellar <u>bursitis</u> [[9]](/library/P_WWoL0)

* <u>Ultrasound</u>: <u>hypoechoic</u> thickening of the <u>patellar tendon</u> [[3]](/library/kHWmq50)[[7]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

## Treatment

Most cases of OSD (> 90%) respond to <u>conservative management</u> and resolve once full bone maturity is reached. [[5]](/library/KHWUr50)




### Approach [[2]](/library/iAWJjL0)[[3]](/library/kHWmq50)[[5]](/library/KHWUr50)




* All patients: Start <u>conservative management</u>.

* If symptoms are severe or persist despite <u>conservative management</u>, consider:

* Immobilizing with a <u>brace</u>, strap, or cast for 3–6 weeks [[12]](/library/MHWMI50)

* Imaging to exclude differential diagnoses of OSD [[6]](/library/py1LTj0)

* If symptoms are refractory and the <u>growth plate</u> has closed, refer for surgical management.





### <u>Conservative management</u> [[2]](/library/iAWJjL0)[[3]](/library/kHWmq50)[[5]](/library/KHWUr50)




* <u>Relative rest</u>: Avoid painful activity, while engaging in physical activity as tolerated. [[11]](/library/OHWIq50)

* <u>NSAIDs</u> (e.g., <u>ibuprofen</u> DOSAGE)

* Ice

* <u>Physical therapy</u> focusing on flexibility and strengthening of the <u>quadriceps</u> and <u>hamstrings</u>





> [!TIP]
> If symptoms are severe or persist despite <u>conservative management</u>, consider immobilizing with a <u>brace</u>, strap, or cast for 3–6 weeks. [[12]](/library/MHWMI50)




> [!WARNING]
> Avoid <u>steroid</u> injections because of the risk of weakening the <u>patellar tendon</u>. [[3]](/library/kHWmq50)[[5]](/library/KHWUr50)




### Surgical management [[3]](/library/kHWmq50)[[5]](/library/KHWUr50)




* Indication: symptoms refractory to <u>conservative management</u> in patients with a closed <u>growth plate</u>

* Method: excision of persistently prominent <u>tibial tuberosity</u> and/or <u>ossicles</u> that have formed in the <u>patellar tendon</u> [[11]](/library/OHWIq50)

---

## Complications

* Genu recurvatum (rare): <u>knee joint</u> deformity characterized by hyperextension in the tibiofemoral <u>joint</u> [[13]](/library/vY1AI20)

* Etiology

* Congenital causes include <u>connective tissue disorders</u> (e.g., <u>Marfan syndrome</u>, <u>Ehlers-Danlos syndrome</u>), <u>physeal arrest</u>, <u>arthrogryposis multiplex congenita</u>, and conditions that affect muscles involved in knee stability (e.g., <u>muscular dystrophy</u>)

* Acquired causes include <u>poliomyelitis</u> and <u>proximal</u> tibial <u>growth plate</u> damage (e.g., due to Osgood-Schlatter disease, <u>osteomyelitis</u>, trauma) [[12]](/library/MHWMI50)

* Clinical features: manifests with <u>knee pain</u>, <u>leg-length discrepancy</u>, poor proprioceptive control, and/or gait disturbances (e.g., extension gait pattern)

* Treatment

* Conservative: taping, knee bracing, gait, and functional training

* Surgical: <u>anterior</u> opening-wedge <u>proximal</u> tibial <u>osteotomy</u> with or without postoperative <u>external fixation</u> with progressive distraction

* Persistently prominent <u>tibial tuberosity</u> [[3]](/library/kHWmq50)

* <u>Ossicle</u> formation in the <u>patellar tendon</u> [[11]](/library/OHWIq50)

* <u>Chronic pain</u>




We list the most important complications. The selection is not exhaustive.
